tldr: Targeting contact-rich industrial assembly with tight tolerances, the authors built "PRISM," a dataset containing over 5,000 multimodal real-robot trajectories. Real-world experiments reveal that even state-of-the-art imitation learning models still face major hurdles in dynamic sorting and precise insertion involving force control.

overview:
Robotic learning has made rapid progress in recent years thanks to large-scale datasets collected in everyday household settings. However, most existing datasets are skewed toward short-horizon, low-contact tasks such as pick-and-place. In contrast, actual assembly work on factory floors involves tight tolerances, friction, and part-to-part engagement—subtle contact dynamics that camera images alone cannot fully capture.

To tackle this challenge, the authors introduce "PRISM," a multimodal dataset specifically tailored for high-precision, contact-rich industrial operations. Spanning more than 25 tasks such as electronic component plugging/unplugging, conveyor-based sorting, and vernier caliper packaging, PRISM gathers over 5,000 teleoperated trajectories totaling more than 45 hours. Its standout feature is high-precision time synchronization across multi-view RGB-D streams, 6-axis force/torque sensors, joint torques, proprioception, and in some tasks, vision-based tactile sensors.

Through real-robot experiments, the authors evaluate representative imitation learning policies—ACT, Diffusion Policy, and π0—investigating the benefits of large-scale pre-training and the impact of different teleoperation interfaces. The results demonstrate that pre-training across the entire dataset boosts robustness against unseen perturbations, and demonstrations collected via an exoskeleton produce far higher quality policies than those collected via VR. At the same time, tasks demanding dynamic tracking or millimeter-level force modulation still exhibit low success rates, clearly highlighting the open challenges for real-world industrial deployment.
contributions: Constructed PRISM, a large-scale real-robot dataset covering over 25 tasks specifically focused on contact-rich, high-precision industrial assembly operations

Achieved rigorously time-synchronized and calibrated multimodal data collection spanning multi-view RGB-D, 6-axis force/torque, joint torques, proprioception, and vision-based tactile sensing (on a subset)
Collected over 5,000 physical trajectories (45+ hours) across three different teleoperation systems (exoskeleton, tracker, and VR) on multiple robot platforms

Quantitatively evaluated the impact of dataset-wide pre-training and different teleoperation interfaces on real-robot task performance using state-of-the-art imitation learning policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, and π0)

sections.heading: From Homes to Factories: Breaking Through the Contact Barrier Beyond Vision Alone
sections.summary: Recent robot learning has advanced rapidly, but existing large-scale datasets are biased toward simple, low-contact tasks. Industrial assembly requires detecting millimeter-scale misalignments and friction, making new multimodal contact-aware benchmarks indispensable.
sections.details:
The field of robot learning has experienced a major paradigm shift through the combination of imitation learning and large datasets gathered in everyday environments. Visuomotor pre-trained models have demonstrated strong generalization on low-contact tasks such as pick-and-place.

However, this success does not directly translate to industrial assembly lines. Factory tasks take place under tight tolerances with tiny clearances, where micro-misalignments, friction-induced binding, and mechanical jamming happen routinely. These phenomena are difficult to detect from camera streams alone and can only be sensed directly through force/torque or tactile sensors. In other words, industrial tasks demand not just "seeing and moving," but long-horizon control that involves "feeling contact forces and compliance-adjusting accordingly."

While prior studies have begun exploring force feedback and multi-view setups (such as REASSEMBLE), none have combined multi-robot support, diverse teleoperation interfaces, and large data scale into a unified dataset. To fill this gap, the authors created PRISM, built around three pillars: industrial-grade synchronization, rich multimodal sensing, and broad mechanical diversity.

sections.heading: The Rise of Generalist Foundation Models vs. The Precision Industrial Gap
sections.summary: While large-scale cross-embodiment datasets drive general-purpose robotic control, research focusing on high-precision industrial manipulation has been constrained by data scale and hardware limits. PRISM bridges this gap.
sections.details:
Robotic manipulation research is shifting rapidly from small, single-task datasets to large datasets spanning diverse embodiments. Efforts such as Open X-Embodiment, RT-1, and BridgeData V2 have shown that massive collections of real-robot trajectories yield powerful visuomotor priors capable of zero-shot transfer to novel instructions and environments.

However, these foundational datasets primarily focus on unstructured home or lab tasks like pick-and-place and tidying. While long-horizon research like FurnitureBench tackles furniture assembly, parts fit loosely, falling short of the tight tolerances required in precision manufacturing.

On the other hand, benchmarks like REASSEMBLE and RH20T leverage NIST task boards (standardized assembly evaluation boards) with 6-axis force/torque sensors to address high-precision assembly. Yet sensor complexity and hardware constraints have limited their data scale to only a few thousand trajectories. PRISM aims to deliver both substantial data scale and diverse hardware configurations, establishing a solid foundation for multimodal learning in precision tasks.

sections.heading: Inside PRISM: Three Teleoperation Modalities and Rigorous Multimodal Sync
sections.summary: PRISM contains over 25 industrial tasks, 5,000+ trajectories, and approximately 27 million visual and tactile frames. By leveraging exoskeleton, tracker, and VR interfaces, it establishes a unified data structure with strictly aligned coordinate frames and timestamps.
sections.details:
PRISM is designed around four core pillars: diversity, multimodality, scale, and task compositionality.

### III-A PRISM Characteristics
Tasks range from NIST task board insertions to conveyor sorting, bearing placement, and product packaging. The hardware platforms include Realman (bimanual arms with a 3-DoF torso), Franka Emika Panda (bimanual arms), and LEJU (humanoid upper body), equipped with end-effectors from standard two-finger parallel grippers to vision-based tactile hands. Data was collected by eight operators across three teleoperation interfaces: an upper-body exoskeleton, Vive trackers, and VR headsets. Episodes also include deliberate human interventions (perturbations) so policies can learn recovery behaviors from contact failures.

Sensing channels include multi-view RGB-D, vision-based tactile (GelSight-style), 6-axis force/torque, joint torques, and robot proprioception (joint angles and end-effector poses) logged at maximum frequencies. Episodes average 25–35 seconds, reflecting the extended time needed for fine contact adjustments in industrial assembly.

### III-B Data Collection and Post-Processing
Three teleoperation pipelines were deployed:
- Exoskeleton setup: Maps operator joint angles directly to the robot's joint space, recording paired human-robot trajectories.
- Tracker setup: Employs bimanual Franka arms with Cartesian tracking and tactile grippers for fine manipulation.
- VR setup: Leverages immersive visual feedback to teleoperate the LEJU humanoid upper body.

In post-processing, a shared timestamp index is established while preserving each sensor's native sampling rate. A transform graph anchored to a global world frame aligns all camera extrinsics and wrist force/torque frames to consistent conventions. All data is serialized into a unified schema compatible with standard libraries like LeRobot.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments Expose Imitation Learning Bottlenecks: Pre-Training Wins and Dynamic Force Limits
sections.summary: ACT, Diffusion Policy, and π0 were evaluated on a bimanual Realman robot. Pre-training on 5,000 trajectories and exoskeleton-based demonstrations proved highly effective, but dynamic picking on a conveyor and micro-force insertion remain difficult hurdles.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted inside an industrial workcell using the same bimanual Realman robot (with 3-DoF torso) seen in the dataset collection.

### IV-A Experimental Setup
Three representative tasks were benchmarked:
- Electronic component plug/unplug: High-precision insertion with millimeter-level clearance
- Packaging a vernier caliper: Packing a precision measurement tool into its fitted case
- Conveyor-based sorting: Dynamic picking of moving objects and sorting them into target bins

Each task used 200 demonstrations to train ACT, Diffusion Policy (DP), and π0 within LeRobot v3.0. The training protocol pre-trains on all 5,000 trajectories for 10% of total steps before fine-tuning on the target task for the remaining 90%.

### IV-B Results and Insights
Key findings include:

- Data Scale (100 vs. 200 demos): Doubling the demonstrations significantly boosted success rates on the two static tasks (plug/unplug and caliper packaging). Larger datasets capture both initial pose variations and micro-corrective actions upon contact. For conveyor sorting, however, gains were limited; visual latency and split-second timing constraints cannot be overcome by simply adding more demonstrations.

- Value of Dataset-Wide Pre-Training: Models pre-trained across PRISM before fine-tuning achieved higher average success rates than models trained from scratch. They demonstrated autonomous recovery behaviors, such as re-approaching parts after slipping or minor collisions.

- Teleoperation Interfaces (Exoskeleton vs. VR): Comparing policies trained on 200 demonstrations from each interface, exoskeleton data yielded markedly higher success rates. VR introduces jerky Cartesian motions and poor depth perception through 2D head displays, whereas the exoskeleton preserves smooth joint-space motion and reliable contact engagement.

- Open Challenges: Even the strongest policies struggled with precise timing on moving objects and closed-loop force regulation during part jamming, leaving overall success rates far from production-ready.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Next Steps: An Open Benchmark for True Industrial Automation
sections.summary: PRISM provides a multimodal dataset addressing high-precision industrial manipulation. Physical robot benchmarks highlight both the strengths and weaknesses of current imitation learning, paving the way for contact estimation and closed-loop force control.
sections.details:
This work introduces PRISM, an open-source dataset modeling precision industrial tasks based on NIST task boards and factory production lines. By logging strictly synchronized multi-view RGB-D, vision-based tactile, 6-axis force/torque, and joint torque data, it offers a solid testbed to the research community.

Comprehensive real-robot evaluations proved the value of large-scale pre-training and high-fidelity exoskeleton demonstrations, while uncovering the limitations of today's imitation learning methods in dynamic handling and tight contact regulation. Key future directions include deeper multimodal integration, explicit contact state estimation, and millisecond-level closed-loop architectures that fully utilize force feedback.

takeaways: Contact-rich, high-precision tasks require time-synchronized multimodal data—including 6-axis force/torque and tactile feedback—rather than vision alone.
Pre-training on a large contact-rich industrial dataset significantly enhances recovery behaviors against misalignments, even with limited task-specific demonstrations.
Teleoperation interface quality matters: exoskeleton demonstrations yield smoother motions and better contact engagement than VR, directly boosting learned policy performance.
Dynamic conveyor sorting and tight mechanical insertions remain formidable challenges even for state-of-the-art imitation learning models (ACT, Diffusion Policy, and π0).
limitations: Vision-based tactile (GelSight-style) sensor data is limited to a subset of episodes rather than available across all trajectories.
Real-world evaluations were conducted on only three representative tasks, leaving comprehensive benchmarking across all 25+ tasks in the dataset incomplete.
Current imitation learning policies operate in an open-loop or low-frequency regime, without introducing fast, adaptive closed-loop control algorithms that actively exploit force feedback.
